concepts.title: Scalars and Vectors in One Dimension
concepts.content_html:
Scalars and Vectors in One Dimension

When you say "the car is going 60 mph," you're describing a scalar — a quantity with magnitude only. But if you say "the car is going 60 mph east," you've added direction, making it a vector.

Scalars vs. Vectors

A scalar is a physical quantity described by a single number (magnitude). Examples include mass, time, speed, distance, and energy.

A vector is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force.

Representing Vectors in 1D

In one dimension, vectors are represented using positive and negative signs to indicate direction. We choose a coordinate system (e.g., right = positive, left = negative) and stick with it throughout a problem.

For example, if rightward is positive:

  • \( v = +5 \text{ m/s} \) means moving to the right at 5 m/s
  • \( v = -3 \text{ m/s} \) means moving to the left at 3 m/s

Distance vs. Displacement

Distance (scalar): the total path length traveled, always positive.

Displacement (vector): the change in position from start to finish.

\[ \Delta x = x_f - x_i \]

where \( x_f \) is the final position and \( x_i \) is the initial position.

Speed vs. Velocity

Speed (scalar): how fast an object moves, always positive.

Velocity (vector): the rate of change of position, includes direction.

\[ v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{x_f - x_i}{t_f - t_i} \]

Key Idea: The sign of velocity tells you the direction of motion. A negative velocity doesn't mean "slowing down" — it means moving in the negative direction.
AP Exam Tip: The AP exam frequently tests whether you can distinguish between distance and displacement, or speed and velocity. Always check whether the question asks for a scalar or vector quantity.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a vector quantity?

hints.text: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
Displacement specifies how far and in what direction an object has moved from its starting point.

solution_steps.text: Vectors have both magnitude and direction. Mass, speed, and distance are all scalars (magnitude only).
Displacement is a vector because it describes both how far and in what direction an object moved. The answer is displacement.

problems.question_html: A person walks 4 m east and then 3 m west. What is the magnitude of the person's displacement?

hints.text: Displacement is the change in position from start to finish, not the total distance traveled.
Taking east as positive: \(\Delta x = +4 + (-3) = +1\) m. The magnitude is 1 m.

solution_steps.text: Let east be positive. The person moves \(+4\) m, then \(-3\) m.
\(\Delta x = +4 + (-3) = +1\) m east. The magnitude of displacement is 1 m.
Note: the total distance traveled is \(4 + 3 = 7\) m, but displacement is only 1 m east.

problems.question_html: A person walks 4 m east and then 3 m west. What is the total distance traveled?

hints.text: Distance is a scalar — add up all the path lengths regardless of direction.

solution_steps.text: Distance is the total path length: \(4 \text{ m} + 3 \text{ m} = 7 \text{ m}\).
Unlike displacement, distance does not depend on direction — it counts every meter traveled.

problems.question_html: An object moves from position \(x = -2\) m to \(x = +6\) m. What is its displacement in meters?

solution_steps.text: \(\Delta x = x_f - x_i = 6 - (-2) = 8\) m in the positive direction.

problems.question_html: A jogger runs 200 m north, then 150 m south, then 100 m north. What is the jogger's displacement?

hints.text: Take north as positive and add the signed displacements.

solution_steps.text: The jogger's displacement is 150 m north. The total distance traveled is \(200 + 150 + 100 = 450\) m.

problems.question_html: A car travels 30 km east in 0.5 hours, then 20 km west in 0.25 hours. What is the average velocity for the entire trip, in km/h? (Take east as positive.)

hints.text: Displacement \(= 30 - 20 = 10\) km east. Total time \(= 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75\) h. Average velocity \(= 10/0.75 \approx 13.3\) km/h.

concepts.title: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration
concepts.content_html:
Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration

A cheetah sprinting across the savanna isn't just fast — it's getting faster. Understanding motion requires three connected quantities: displacement, velocity, and acceleration.

Displacement

Displacement is the change in position of an object:

\[ \Delta x = x_f - x_i \]

It's a vector — it has both magnitude and direction.

Velocity

Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time:

\[ v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} \]

Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a single moment — the slope of the position-time graph at that instant.

Acceleration

Average acceleration is the rate of change of velocity:

\[ a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_f - v_i}{t_f - t_i} \]

Instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the velocity-time graph at a particular instant.

Variable Definitions

  • \( \Delta x \) — displacement (m)
  • \( \Delta t \) — time interval (s)
  • \( v \) — velocity (m/s)
  • \( a \) — acceleration (m/s²)

Signs of Acceleration

Acceleration tells you how velocity is changing:

  • If \( v \) and \( a \) have the same sign, the object is speeding up.
  • If \( v \) and \( a \) have opposite signs, the object is slowing down.
Key Idea: Acceleration is NOT the same as velocity. An object can have a large velocity and zero acceleration (constant speed), or zero velocity and nonzero acceleration (momentarily stopped but about to move).
AP Exam Tip: "Negative acceleration" does NOT automatically mean "slowing down." If an object moves in the negative direction with negative acceleration, it is speeding up.

problems.question_html: A car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its average acceleration?

hints.text: Average acceleration \(= \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). "From rest" means \(v_i = 0\).

problems.question_html: An object moves with velocity \(v = -6\) m/s and acceleration \(a = -2\) m/s². Is the object speeding up or slowing down?

choices.text: Speeding up, because the acceleration is negative
Slowing down, because the acceleration is negative
Speeding up, because velocity and acceleration have the same sign
Slowing down, because velocity and acceleration have the same sign

hints.text: Compare the signs of velocity and acceleration. Same sign = speeding up; opposite signs = slowing down.
Both \(v\) and \(a\) are negative (same sign), so the object speeds up in the negative direction.

solution_steps.text: \(v = -6\) m/s and \(a = -2\) m/s² have the same sign (both negative).
When velocity and acceleration have the same sign, the object is speeding up. The object moves faster in the negative direction.

problems.question_html: A bicycle slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 2 seconds. What is the average acceleration in m/s²?

solution_steps.text: The negative sign indicates the acceleration is opposite to the direction of motion — the bicycle is slowing down.

problems.question_html: An object has a velocity of 10 m/s and an acceleration of 0 m/s². What is the velocity after 5 seconds, in m/s?

hints.text: Zero acceleration means the velocity does not change.
With \(a = 0\), the velocity stays at 10 m/s regardless of time.

solution_steps.text: If \(a = 0\), velocity is constant. After 5 seconds the velocity is still 10 m/s.

problems.question_html: A car travels 100 m in 10 s, stops for 5 s, then travels 50 m in 5 s, all in the same direction. What is the average velocity for the entire trip?

hints.text: Average velocity = total displacement / total time. Include the time stopped.
Total displacement = 150 m. Total time = 10 + 5 + 5 = 20 s. \(v_{\text{avg}} = 150/20 = 7.5\) m/s.

problems.question_html: A ball is thrown straight up with an initial velocity of 15 m/s. At the top of its path, what are the velocity and acceleration? (Take upward as positive, \(g = 10\) m/s².)

hints.text: At the highest point, the ball momentarily stops — what is the velocity at that instant?
Velocity = 0 m/s at the top. Acceleration due to gravity is always \(-10\) m/s² (downward), even when the ball is momentarily at rest.

solution_steps.text: At the top: velocity \(= 0\) m/s (momentarily at rest).
Acceleration \(= -10\) m/s² (gravity acts downward at all times, including at the peak).
A common misconception is that acceleration is zero at the top — it is not. If it were, the ball would remain suspended.

concepts.title: Representing Motion
concepts.content_html:
Representing Motion

A picture is worth a thousand equations. Physicists use graphs and equations to represent motion, and each representation tells you something different about how an object moves.

Position-Time Graphs

On a position vs. time graph:

  • The slope equals the velocity.
  • A straight line means constant velocity.
  • A curved line means the velocity is changing (acceleration).
  • A horizontal line means the object is at rest.

Velocity-Time Graphs

On a velocity vs. time graph:

  • The slope equals the acceleration.
  • The area under the curve equals the displacement.
  • A horizontal line means constant velocity (zero acceleration).
  • A line crossing the time axis means the object changes direction.

Kinematic Equations (Constant Acceleration)

When acceleration is constant, these four equations relate position, velocity, acceleration, and time:

\[ v = v_0 + at \]

\[ \Delta x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 \]

\[ v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x \]

\[ \Delta x = \tfrac{1}{2}(v_0 + v)t \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( v_0 \) — initial velocity (m/s)
  • \( v \) — final velocity (m/s)
  • \( a \) — acceleration (m/s²)
  • \( t \) — time (s)
  • \( \Delta x \) — displacement (m)

Free Fall

Free fall is motion under the influence of gravity alone. Near Earth's surface:

\[ a = -g = -9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 \approx -10 \text{ m/s}^2 \]

(taking upward as positive). All kinematic equations apply with \( a = -g \).

Key Idea: Choose the kinematic equation that contains the three known quantities and the one unknown. Each equation "leaves out" one variable.
AP Exam Tip: The AP equation sheet provides the kinematic equations. Know which variable each equation omits so you can quickly select the right one.

problems.question_html: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(3 \text{ m/s}^2\) for 4 seconds. What is the car's final velocity?
On a velocity-time graph, what does the area under the curve represent?

hints.text: Think about what you get when you multiply velocity by time.
Area = velocity × time = displacement. Note: area below the time axis counts as negative displacement.

solution_steps.text: The area under a velocity-time graph equals the displacement of the object.
This follows from \(\Delta x = v \cdot \Delta t\), and the area represents the sum of all such products.

problems.question_html: A ball is dropped from rest. How far does it fall in 3 seconds? Use \(g = 10\) m/s². Give your answer in meters.

hints.text: Use \(\Delta x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\) with \(v_0 = 0\) and \(a = g = 10\) m/s² downward.

solution_steps.text: Taking downward as positive: \(\Delta x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \frac{1}{2}(10)(3^2) = 45\) m.

problems.question_html: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of \(4 \text{ m/s}^2\). How far does it travel before stopping? Give your answer in meters.

hints.text: The car stops when \(v = 0\). Use \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x\).

problems.question_html: A stone is thrown straight up with an initial velocity of 30 m/s. Using \(g = 10\) m/s², what maximum height does it reach?

hints.text: At max height, \(v = 0\). Use \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x\) with \(a = -10\) m/s².

problems.question_html: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over a distance of 200 m. What is the acceleration in m/s²?

hints.text: Use \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x\). You know \(v, v_0,\) and \(\Delta x\).

problems.question_html: A car starts at rest and accelerates at \(2 \text{ m/s}^2\) for 6 seconds, then travels at constant velocity for 4 seconds. What is the total displacement? Give your answer in meters.

hints.text: Break the problem into two phases. First find the velocity at the end of phase 1.
Phase 1: \(\Delta x_1 = \frac{1}{2}(2)(36) = 36\) m, final velocity = 12 m/s. Phase 2: \(\Delta x_2 = 12(4) = 48\) m. Total = 84 m.

problems.question_html:
A ball is thrown vertically upward at 25 m/s from ground level. Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

(a) How long does it take to reach the highest point?

(b) What is the total time in the air (until it returns to the launch height)?

(c) Explain why the time going up equals the time coming down.
problems.sample_answer: (a) At the top, v = 0. Using v = v₀ + at: 0 = 25 + (-10)t → t = 2.5 s. (b) By symmetry, total time = 2 × 2.5 = 5.0 s. (c) The acceleration is constant, so the motion is symmetric — the ball decelerates going up and accelerates at the same rate coming down.
rubric: Correctly finds time to top: t = 2.5 s using v = v₀ + at
Determines total time = 5.0 s using symmetry or kinematic equation
Explains symmetry: constant acceleration means equal time up and down

hints.text: At the highest point, the velocity is zero. Use \(v = v_0 + at\) with \(v = 0\).
\(0 = 25 + (-10)t \Rightarrow t = 2.5\) s to the top. By symmetry of projectile motion, total time = 5.0 s.

solution_steps.text: (b) Total time \(= 2 \times 2.5 = 5.0\) s. Alternatively, use \(\Delta x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = 0\): \(25t - 5t^2 = 0 \Rightarrow t(25 - 5t) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 5\) s.
(c) With constant acceleration, the velocity change is the same magnitude in equal time intervals. Going up, the ball loses speed at the same rate it gains speed coming down, so the times are equal.

problems.correct_answer: (a) At the top, v = 0. Using v = v₀ + at: 0 = 25 + (-10)t → t = 2.5 s. (b) By symmetry, total time = 2 × 2.5 = 5.0 s. (c) The acceleration is constant, so the motion is symmetric — the ball decelerates going up and accelerates at the same rate coming down.

concepts.title: Reference Frames and Relative Motion
concepts.content_html:
Reference Frames and Relative Motion

If you're sitting on a moving train, are you moving or stationary? The answer depends on your reference frame.

What Is a Reference Frame?

A reference frame is a coordinate system attached to an observer. Different observers can measure different velocities for the same object, and all measurements are equally valid.

Relative Velocity in 1D

The velocity of object A relative to object B is:

\[ \vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B \]

where \( \vec{v}_A \) and \( \vec{v}_B \) are measured in the same reference frame (e.g., the ground).

Example

Car A travels east at 30 m/s. Car B travels east at 20 m/s. The velocity of A relative to B:

\[ v_{A/B} = 30 - 20 = 10 \text{ m/s east} \]

From the perspective of someone in Car B, Car A appears to move forward at 10 m/s.

If they travel in opposite directions (A east at 30, B west at 20):

\[ v_{A/B} = 30 - (-20) = 50 \text{ m/s east} \]

Galilean Relativity

The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) reference frames. An experiment performed on a smoothly moving train gives the same results as one performed on the ground.

Key Idea: There is no absolute reference frame. All motion is relative — you must always specify "relative to what."
AP Exam Tip: Relative velocity problems often appear as multi-step problems. Set up a clear sign convention first and apply \(\vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B\) consistently.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Reference Frames and Relative Motion

problems.question_html: Two cars travel in the same direction. Car A moves at 25 m/s and Car B moves at 15 m/s. What is the velocity of Car A relative to Car B?

choices.text: 10 m/s in the direction of motion
10 m/s opposite to the direction of motion

hints.text: \(v_{A/B} = 25 - 15 = 10\) m/s in the same direction as motion.

solution_steps.text: Car A appears to move forward at 10 m/s from Car B's perspective.

problems.question_html: Two trains approach each other, each traveling at 20 m/s. What is the velocity of one train relative to the other?

hints.text: If they approach each other, their velocities have opposite signs. Let one be +20 and the other −20.

solution_steps.text: Let rightward be positive. Train A: \(+20\) m/s. Train B: \(-20\) m/s.
\(v_{A/B} = 20 - (-20) = 40\) m/s. Each train sees the other approaching at 40 m/s.

problems.question_html: A boat travels at 5 m/s relative to the water. The river flows at 3 m/s. If the boat moves upstream, what is its speed relative to the ground, in m/s?

hints.text: Upstream means the boat moves against the current. Subtract the river speed.

solution_steps.text: The boat moves at 5 m/s relative to water, but the water moves 3 m/s in the opposite direction.

problems.question_html: A person walks at 1.5 m/s on a moving walkway that travels at 2.0 m/s in the same direction. What is the person's speed relative to the ground, in m/s?

hints.text: When moving in the same direction, add the speeds.

solution_steps.text: The person's velocity relative to ground = velocity relative to walkway + velocity of walkway relative to ground.

problems.question_html: Car A travels north at 30 m/s. Car B travels south at 20 m/s. A passenger in Car B throws a ball forward (south) at 5 m/s relative to Car B. What is the velocity of the ball relative to Car A? (Take north as positive.)

hints.text: First find the ball's velocity relative to the ground, then find it relative to Car A.
Ball relative to ground: \(-20 + (-5) = -25\) m/s. Ball relative to A: \(-25 - 30 = -55\) m/s = 55 m/s south.

solution_steps.text: Car B velocity (ground frame): \(-20\) m/s. Ball relative to B: \(-5\) m/s.
Ball relative to A: \(-25 - (+30) = -55\) m/s = 55 m/s south.

problems.question_html: A plane flies at 200 m/s relative to the air. A wind blows at 50 m/s from west to east. If the plane flies directly east, what is its ground speed in m/s?

hints.text: The plane and wind move in the same direction (east). Add the velocities.

solution_steps.text: Plane velocity relative to air: 200 m/s east. Wind velocity: 50 m/s east.
Plane velocity relative to ground \(= 200 + 50 = 250\) m/s east.

problems.question_html: A passenger on a train moving at 25 m/s east drops a ball. Describe the path of the ball as seen by (a) the passenger and (b) a person standing on the ground. Explain why the descriptions differ.
problems.sample_answer: (a) The passenger sees the ball fall straight down because both the ball and passenger share the same horizontal velocity. (b) The ground observer sees the ball follow a parabolic path — it moves forward (east) while falling, because it retains the train's horizontal velocity. The descriptions differ because the observers are in different reference frames.
rubric: Correctly describes the straight-down path in the train's frame
Correctly describes the parabolic path in the ground frame
Explains the difference using reference frames and the ball retaining the train's horizontal velocity

hints.text: Think about what horizontal velocity the ball has the moment it is released.
The ball keeps the train's horizontal velocity (25 m/s east) after release. In the train's frame, this is zero relative motion horizontally.

solution_steps.text: (a) In the train's frame, the ball has no horizontal velocity relative to the passenger, so it falls straight down.
(b) In the ground frame, the ball has horizontal velocity 25 m/s east (from the train) plus downward acceleration due to gravity, creating a parabolic trajectory.
The difference arises because motion looks different in different reference frames. Both descriptions are correct — neither is more "real" than the other.

problems.correct_answer: (a) The passenger sees the ball fall straight down because both the ball and passenger share the same horizontal velocity. (b) The ground observer sees the ball follow a parabolic path — it moves forward (east) while falling, because it retains the train's horizontal velocity. The descriptions differ because the observers are in different reference frames.

concepts.title: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
concepts.content_html:
Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

When you kick a soccer ball at an angle, it moves both forward and upward at the same time. Two-dimensional motion requires us to treat the horizontal and vertical components independently.

Vector Components

Any vector can be broken into perpendicular components using trigonometry:

\[ A_x = A \cos\theta \qquad A_y = A \sin\theta \]

where \( A \) is the magnitude and \( \theta \) is the angle measured from the positive x-axis.

To find the magnitude and direction from components:

\[ A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2} \qquad \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right) \]

Adding Vectors

To add vectors, add their components separately:

\[ \vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} \Rightarrow R_x = A_x + B_x, \quad R_y = A_y + B_y \]

Projectile Motion

A projectile is any object moving under the influence of gravity alone (no air resistance). The key insight:

  • Horizontal: no acceleration → constant velocity → \( x = v_{0x} t \)
  • Vertical: acceleration \( g \) downward → use kinematic equations

The two directions are independent — horizontal motion doesn't affect vertical motion.

\[ v_{0x} = v_0 \cos\theta \qquad v_{0y} = v_0 \sin\theta \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( v_{0x}, v_{0y} \) — initial velocity components (m/s)
  • \( \theta \) — launch angle (degrees or radians)
  • \( g = 9.8 \approx 10 \text{ m/s}^2\) — acceleration due to gravity
Key Idea: In projectile motion, the horizontal and vertical components are completely independent. Treat them as two separate 1D problems connected only by time.
AP Exam Tip: When solving projectile problems, always start by listing the known quantities for horizontal and vertical directions separately. Time is the variable that links them.

problems.question_html: A vector has magnitude 10 and makes a 30° angle with the positive x-axis. What is its x-component?
A ball is launched horizontally from a 20 m high cliff at 15 m/s. How long does it take to hit the ground? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

hints.text: The time to fall depends only on the vertical motion. Use \(\Delta y = \frac{1}{2}gt^2\) with \(v_{0y} = 0\).

solution_steps.text: \(20 = 5t^2 \Rightarrow t = 2.0\) s. The horizontal velocity (15 m/s) does not affect the fall time.

problems.question_html: Two vectors have components \(\vec{A} = (3, 4)\) and \(\vec{B} = (1, -2)\). What is the magnitude of \(\vec{A} + \vec{B}\)? Give your answer to one decimal place.

hints.text: Add components: \(R_x = A_x + B_x\), \(R_y = A_y + B_y\). Then find the magnitude.

problems.question_html: A projectile is launched at 45° with initial speed 20 m/s. What is the initial horizontal velocity component, in m/s? Round to one decimal place.
A ball is launched at 60° above the horizontal with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Using \(g = 10\) m/s², what is the maximum height reached?

hints.text: Find \(v_{0y} = v_0 \sin 60°\), then use \(v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2g\Delta y\) with \(v_y = 0\) at the top.

problems.question_html: A rescue package is dropped from a helicopter flying horizontally at 40 m/s at an altitude of 80 m. Using \(g = 10\) m/s², how far ahead of the target should the pilot release the package?

hints.text: The package is "dropped" so \(v_{0y} = 0\), but it has horizontal velocity 40 m/s from the helicopter.
Fall time: \(80 = \frac{1}{2}(10)t^2 \Rightarrow t = 4\) s. Horizontal distance \(= 40(4) = 160\) m.

solution_steps.text: Horizontal: \(x = 40(4) = 160\) m. The pilot should release the package 160 m before the target.

problems.question_html: A ball is launched horizontally at 10 m/s from a 45 m high cliff. Using \(g = 10\) m/s², how far from the base of the cliff does it land? Give your answer in meters.

hints.text: Find the fall time from vertical motion, then multiply by horizontal velocity.

solution_steps.text: Horizontal: \(x = v_{0x} t = 10(3) = 30\) m from the base.

problems.question_html:
A projectile is launched at angle \(\theta\) with initial speed \(v_0\) from level ground. Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

(a) Derive an expression for the range (horizontal distance) in terms of \(v_0\), \(\theta\), and \(g\).

(b) At what angle is the range maximized?

(c) Explain why 30° and 60° give the same range.
problems.sample_answer: (a) Time of flight: 2v₀sinθ/g. Range: R = v₀cosθ × (2v₀sinθ/g) = v₀²sin(2θ)/g. (b) Maximum when sin(2θ) = 1, so 2θ = 90° → θ = 45°. (c) sin(2×30°) = sin(60°) and sin(2×60°) = sin(120°) = sin(60°). The two angles are complementary and give equal sin(2θ).
rubric: Derives range formula R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g correctly
Identifies θ = 45° as the angle for maximum range
Explains complementary angle symmetry using sin(2θ) = sin(180° - 2θ)

hints.text: Find total time using vertical motion (ball returns to launch height). Then multiply by \(v_{0x}\).

solution_steps.text: (c) \(\sin(2 \times 30°) = \sin 60°\) and \(\sin(2 \times 60°) = \sin 120° = \sin 60°\). Complementary angles give the same value of \(\sin(2\theta)\), hence the same range.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Time of flight: 2v₀sinθ/g. Range: R = v₀cosθ × (2v₀sinθ/g) = v₀²sin(2θ)/g. (b) Maximum when sin(2θ) = 1, so 2θ = 90° → θ = 45°. (c) sin(2×30°) = sin(60°) and sin(2×60°) = sin(120°) = sin(60°). The two angles are complementary and give equal sin(2θ).

concepts.title: Systems and Center of Mass
concepts.content_html:
Systems and Center of Mass

When a firework explodes in the air, the pieces fly in all directions — but the center of mass of all the pieces continues along the same parabolic path as if the explosion never happened.

What Is a System?

A system is any collection of objects that we choose to analyze together. The boundary of a system is a deliberate choice — different system boundaries lead to different analyses.

Center of Mass

The center of mass (COM) is the average position of all the mass in a system, weighted by mass:

\[ x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + \cdots}{m_1 + m_2 + \cdots} = \frac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i} \]

For a two-object system:

\[ x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2} \]

Motion of the Center of Mass

The center of mass moves as if all the mass were concentrated at that point and all external forces acted there:

\[ \vec{F}_{\text{net, ext}} = M \vec{a}_{\text{cm}} \]

where \( M \) is the total mass. Internal forces (forces between objects within the system) do NOT affect the motion of the center of mass.

Variable Definitions

  • \( x_{\text{cm}} \) — center of mass position (m)
  • \( m_i \) — mass of object \(i\) (kg)
  • \( x_i \) — position of object \(i\) (m)
  • \( M \) — total mass of system (kg)
Key Idea: The center of mass of an isolated system moves with constant velocity. Only external forces can change the motion of the center of mass.
AP Exam Tip: When asked about the motion of a system, focus on external forces only. Internal forces always come in Newton's third law pairs and cancel within the system.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Systems and Center of Mass

problems.question_html: A 2 kg object is at \(x = 0\) m and a 6 kg object is at \(x = 4\) m. Where is the center of mass?

solution_steps.text: The center of mass is closer to the heavier object, as expected.

problems.question_html: Which forces affect the motion of the center of mass of a system?

choices.text: Both internal and external forces equally
Neither — the center of mass always moves at constant velocity

hints.text: Internal forces come in Newton's third law pairs. What happens when you add them?
Internal forces cancel in pairs, so only external forces affect the center of mass acceleration: \(\vec{F}_{\text{net,ext}} = M\vec{a}_{\text{cm}}\).

solution_steps.text: Internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's third law) and cancel within the system.
Only external forces can change the velocity of the center of mass.

problems.question_html: A 3 kg ball at \(x = 1\) m and a 5 kg ball at \(x = 5\) m. What is the x-coordinate of the center of mass, in meters?
Two objects with equal mass are located at \(x = 2\) m and \(x = 8\) m. Where is the center of mass, in meters?

hints.text: For equal masses, the center of mass is at the midpoint.

problems.question_html: A 60 kg person stands at one end of a 4 m long, 20 kg boat on frictionless water. The person walks 3 m toward the other end. How far does the boat move?

hints.text: No external horizontal forces, so the center of mass doesn't move. Set up \(m_1 \Delta x_1 + m_2 \Delta x_2 = 0\).

\(60(3 - d) + 20(-d) \cdot \ldots\) Actually: \(60 \cdot d_{\text{person}} = 20 \cdot d_{\text{boat}}\) in opposite directions, and \(d_{\text{person}} + d_{\text{boat}} = 3\). So \(d_{\text{boat}} = \frac{60 \times 3}{80} = 2.25\) m.

solution_steps.text: No external horizontal forces → center of mass stays fixed.
Person moves 3 m relative to boat. If boat moves distance \(d\) opposite: person moves \(3 - d\) relative to ground.

problems.question_html: A 4 kg object at \(x = 0\) and a 1 kg object at \(x = 10\) m are connected by a spring on a frictionless surface. If the 4 kg object moves to \(x = 2\) m, where is the 1 kg object?

hints.text: No external horizontal forces → COM stays fixed. Find the initial COM first.
Initial COM: \(\frac{4(0)+1(10)}{5} = 2\) m. After: \(\frac{4(2)+1(x)}{5} = 2 \Rightarrow 8 + x = 10 \Rightarrow x = 2\) m.

solution_steps.text: COM is fixed: \(\frac{4(2)+1(x_2)}{5} = 2 \Rightarrow 8 + x_2 = 10 \Rightarrow x_2 = 2\) m.

problems.question_html: Three masses are arranged: 1 kg at (0, 0), 2 kg at (3, 0), and 3 kg at (0, 4). What is the y-coordinate of the center of mass?

A firework of mass 2 kg is launched vertically. At its highest point (50 m), it explodes into two equal pieces. One piece has zero velocity immediately after the explosion. Where does the center of mass of the two pieces land relative to the launch point? Explain your reasoning.
problems.sample_answer: The center of mass lands directly below the highest point — at the launch point (x = 0). Since the only external force is gravity (vertical), the horizontal position of the center of mass doesn't change. The explosion is an internal force and cannot alter the COM trajectory.
rubric: States that the center of mass lands at the launch point (directly below the explosion)
Explains that the explosion is an internal force and doesn't affect COM motion
Notes that only gravity (external) acts, and it's vertical, so horizontal COM doesn't change

hints.text: The explosion is an internal force. What does that mean for the center of mass trajectory?
Internal forces don't change the COM motion. The COM continues on the same trajectory as if the firework never exploded — straight down from the highest point.

solution_steps.text: The explosion is an internal force — it cannot change the motion of the center of mass.
Before the explosion, the firework was launched vertically, so the COM has no horizontal velocity.
The COM continues falling straight down under gravity and lands at the launch point (x = 0).

problems.correct_answer: The center of mass lands directly below the highest point — at the launch point (x = 0). Since the only external force is gravity (vertical), the horizontal position of the center of mass doesn't change. The explosion is an internal force and cannot alter the COM trajectory.

concepts.title: Forces and Free-Body Diagrams
concepts.content_html:
Forces and Free-Body Diagrams

Every time you push a door, pull a wagon, or simply stand on the ground, you are exerting and experiencing forces. A force is a push or pull on an object due to its interaction with another object.

Types of Forces

  • Gravitational force (weight): \( F_g = mg \), always directed downward
  • Normal force (\(F_N\)): perpendicular to the contact surface, prevents objects from passing through each other
  • Tension (\(T\)): force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable; always pulls
  • Friction (\(f\)): opposes relative motion or the tendency of motion between surfaces
  • Spring force: force exerted by a compressed or stretched spring
  • Applied force: any external push or pull

Free-Body Diagrams (FBDs)

A free-body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object, represented as arrows originating from the object's center. Steps to draw one:

  1. Isolate the object of interest
  2. Identify all forces acting ON that object (not forces it exerts)
  3. Draw each force as an arrow showing magnitude and direction
  4. Label each force

Contact vs. Non-Contact Forces

Contact forces require physical touch: normal force, friction, tension, applied force.

Non-contact forces act at a distance: gravity, electromagnetic forces.

Key Idea: A free-body diagram shows only forces acting ON the object, not forces the object exerts on other things. Every force has an agent — ask "what is pushing/pulling this object?"
AP Exam Tip: The AP exam frequently asks you to draw or identify correct FBDs. Common mistakes: including forces the object exerts on others, forgetting the normal force, or drawing friction in the wrong direction.

problems.question_html: A book sits on a table. How many forces act on the book?

hints.text: Think about what pulls the book down and what keeps it from falling through the table.
Gravity pulls the book down; the normal force from the table pushes it up. Two forces.

solution_steps.text: Two forces act on the book: (1) gravitational force (weight) downward, (2) normal force from the table upward.
These two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the book is in equilibrium.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a non-contact force?

hints.text: A non-contact force acts without physical touch between objects.
Gravity acts between any two masses regardless of whether they touch. Tension, normal force, and friction all require contact.

solution_steps.text: Gravity is the only non-contact force listed. It acts at a distance between any two objects with mass.

problems.question_html: A 5 kg object rests on a flat surface. What is the normal force on the object, in newtons? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

hints.text: The object is in equilibrium on a flat surface, so the normal force equals the weight.

solution_steps.text: On a flat surface in equilibrium: \(F_N = mg = 5 \times 10 = 50\) N upward.

problems.question_html: A 10 kg box is pushed across a floor with an applied force of 40 N. Friction exerts 15 N opposing the motion. What is the net force on the box, in newtons?

hints.text: Net force = applied force minus friction (in the horizontal direction).
\(F_{\text{net}} = 40 - 15 = 25\) N in the direction of the push.

solution_steps.text: Vertical forces (weight and normal) balance, so they don't contribute to the net horizontal force.

problems.question_html: A 20 kg block hangs from two ropes that make angles of 30° and 60° with the horizontal ceiling. What is the tension in the rope at 60°? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

hints.text: Set up equilibrium equations: \(\sum F_x = 0\) and \(\sum F_y = 0\). Use the angles to find components of each tension.
From x-equilibrium, \(T_1 = 0.577 T_2\). Substitute into the y-equation and solve for \(T_2\).

solution_steps.text: \(1.155\,T_2 = 200\) → \(T_2 \approx 173\) N. The tension in the rope at 60° is approximately 173 N.

concepts.title: Newton's Third Law
concepts.content_html:
Newton's Third Law

When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with exactly the same force. This isn't a coincidence — it's Newton's Third Law.

The Law

Newton's Third Law: If object A exerts a force on object B, then object B exerts a force on object A that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

\[ \vec{F}_{A \text{ on } B} = -\vec{F}_{B \text{ on } A} \]

Key Properties of Third-Law Pairs

  • They act on different objects
  • They are the same type of force (e.g., both gravitational, both contact)
  • They are always equal in magnitude, regardless of the masses of the objects
  • They exist simultaneously — one cannot exist without the other

Common Misconception

"The heavier truck exerts more force on the small car in a collision." Wrong! Both experience the same force. The car has greater acceleration because it has less mass (\(a = F/m\)).

Key Idea: Third-law force pairs always act on different objects. They never cancel each other because they don't act on the same object. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.
AP Exam Tip: To identify a Newton's third law pair, check: (1) Are the forces on different objects? (2) Are they the same type of force? (3) Are they equal and opposite? All three must be true.
concepts.content_raw: Newton's Third Law

problems.question_html: A person pushes on a wall with a force of 50 N. What force does the wall exert on the person?

hints.text: Newton's Third Law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
The wall pushes back on the person with 50 N in the opposite direction.

solution_steps.text: By Newton's Third Law, the wall exerts 50 N on the person in the opposite direction.

problems.question_html: A 1000 kg car collides with a 3000 kg truck. Which vehicle experiences the greater force during the collision?

choices.text: The truck, because it has more mass
The car, because it has less mass

hints.text: Newton's Third Law applies regardless of the masses of the objects.
Both experience the same magnitude of force. The car has greater acceleration because \(a = F/m\) and its mass is smaller.

solution_steps.text: By Newton's Third Law, the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
The car experiences greater acceleration (and more damage) because it has less mass, not because the force is different.

problems.question_html: A book rests on a table. The weight of the book and the normal force from the table are equal and opposite. Are they a Newton's Third Law pair? (Answer yes or no.)
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: Newton's Third Law pairs act on different objects and are the same type of force. Are the weight and normal force the same type?
Weight is gravitational (Earth pulls book). Normal force is contact (table pushes book). They're different types and both act on the book — not a third-law pair.

solution_steps.text: No. Both forces act on the same object (the book), so they cannot be a third-law pair.
The third-law partner of the book's weight is the gravitational force the book exerts on the Earth.
The third-law partner of the normal force is the force the book pushes down on the table.

problems.question_html: A horse pulls a cart forward. The cart pulls the horse backward with the same force. Why does the system move forward?
problems.correct_answer: friction

hints.text: The third-law forces act on different objects. What other force acts on the horse?
The horse pushes backward on the ground; the ground pushes the horse forward (friction). If this friction exceeds the cart's resistance, the system accelerates.

solution_steps.text: The third-law pair (horse-on-cart and cart-on-horse) acts on different objects.
The horse also pushes backward on the ground, and friction from the ground pushes the horse forward.
The net external force on the horse-cart system comes from the ground's friction minus any resistive forces on the cart.

problems.question_html: An astronaut (80 kg) pushes off a spacecraft (2000 kg) with a force of 100 N. What is the acceleration of the astronaut, in m/s²?

hints.text: The spacecraft pushes back on the astronaut with 100 N (Newton's Third Law). Use \(a = F/m\).

solution_steps.text: By Newton's Third Law, the spacecraft exerts 100 N on the astronaut.
The spacecraft's acceleration is \(100/2000 = 0.05\) m/s² — much smaller due to its larger mass.

problems.question_html: Two ice skaters face each other. Skater A (50 kg) pushes skater B (75 kg) and skater A accelerates at 3 m/s². What is skater B's acceleration, in m/s²?

hints.text: Find the force first using skater A's mass and acceleration, then apply it to skater B.

solution_steps.text: By Newton's Third Law, the same 150 N acts on B.

concepts.title: Newton's First Law
concepts.content_html:
Newton's First Law

A hockey puck sliding on frictionless ice will continue moving in a straight line forever. It doesn't need a force to keep moving — it needs a force to stop.

The Law

Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion with constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force.

\[ \text{If } \vec{F}_{\text{net}} = 0, \text{ then } \vec{v} = \text{constant} \]

Inertia

Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion. Mass is a measure of inertia — more mass means more resistance to acceleration.

Equilibrium

An object is in equilibrium when the net force on it is zero. This can mean:

  • Static equilibrium: at rest and staying at rest
  • Dynamic equilibrium: moving at constant velocity

In both cases, \(\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = 0\) and \(\vec{a} = 0\).

Key Idea: An object does NOT need a force to keep moving. It needs a force to change its motion (speed up, slow down, or change direction).
AP Exam Tip: If an object moves at constant velocity, the net force is zero — even if multiple forces act on it. They simply balance out.

problems.question_html: A car moves at a constant 25 m/s on a straight road. What is the net force on the car?

choices.text: Greater than zero, in the forward direction

hints.text: Constant velocity means zero acceleration. What does Newton's First Law say?
If velocity is constant, the net force must be zero. The engine force and friction balance.

solution_steps.text: Constant velocity → zero acceleration → net force = 0 (Newton's First Law).
The engine provides a forward force that exactly balances friction and air resistance.

problems.question_html: Which of the following best describes inertia?

choices.text: The force needed to start an object moving
The tendency of an object to resist changes in motion
The rate at which an object changes velocity
The energy an object has due to its motion

hints.text: Inertia is related to mass — heavier objects have more of it.
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion. Mass is the measure of inertia.

solution_steps.text: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion (Newton's First Law).
Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia.

problems.question_html: A box is pushed across a floor at constant velocity by a 30 N horizontal force. What is the friction force, in newtons?

hints.text: Constant velocity means zero net force.
If the net force is zero, friction must equal the applied force: 30 N.

solution_steps.text: Constant velocity → \(F_{\text{net}} = 0\) → friction = applied force = 30 N.

problems.question_html: An object at rest has no forces acting on it. True or false?
problems.correct_answer: false

hints.text: Think about a book on a table — it's at rest. Are there really no forces?
An object at rest has zero NET force, but individual forces can still act on it (e.g., weight and normal force).

solution_steps.text: False. An object at rest has zero net force, but multiple forces can act on it and cancel out (equilibrium).

problems.question_html: A 5 kg object moves in a straight line at 10 m/s. Three forces act on it: 20 N forward, 12 N backward, and 8 N backward. Is the object accelerating?

choices.text: No, it moves at constant velocity

hints.text: Net force \(= 20 - 12 - 8 = 0\) N. Zero net force → constant velocity → no acceleration.

solution_steps.text: By Newton's First Law, the object continues at constant velocity (10 m/s). No acceleration.

problems.question_html: A 2000 kg elevator moves upward at constant speed. What is the tension in the cable, in newtons? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

hints.text: Constant speed means net force = 0. The tension must balance the weight.

concepts.title: Newton's Second Law
concepts.content_html:
Newton's Second Law

Newton's Second Law is the most important equation in mechanics. It connects force, mass, and acceleration in one powerful statement.

The Law

\[ \vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\vec{a} \]

The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. The acceleration is always in the same direction as the net force.

Applying Newton's Second Law

Steps to solve problems:

  1. Draw a free-body diagram
  2. Choose a coordinate system
  3. Write \(\sum F_x = ma_x\) and \(\sum F_y = ma_y\)
  4. Solve for the unknown

Variable Definitions

  • \( F_{\text{net}} \) — net (total) force (N)
  • \( m \) — mass (kg)
  • \( a \) — acceleration (m/s²)

Weight vs. Mass

Mass (kg) is the amount of matter; it's the same everywhere.

Weight (N) is the gravitational force: \( W = mg \). It depends on location.

Key Idea: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass. Double the force → double the acceleration. Double the mass → half the acceleration.
AP Exam Tip: Always use the NET force in \(F = ma\), not just one of the forces. A common error is forgetting friction or weight components.

problems.question_html: A 10 kg box is pushed with a net force of 40 N. What is its acceleration?
A 5 kg object accelerates at \(3 \text{ m/s}^2\). A 15 kg object experiences the same net force. What is the 15 kg object's acceleration?

hints.text: First find the force using the 5 kg object, then apply it to the 15 kg object.

solution_steps.text: Same force on 15 kg: \(a = 15/15 = 1\) m/s². Triple the mass → one-third the acceleration.

problems.question_html: What net force is needed to accelerate a 2000 kg car at \(1.5 \text{ m/s}^2\)? Give your answer in newtons.
A 50 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at \(2 \text{ m/s}^2\). What does the scale read, in newtons? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

hints.text: The scale reads the normal force. Apply \(\sum F_y = ma_y\): \(N - mg = ma\).

solution_steps.text: The person feels heavier because the elevator accelerates upward.

problems.question_html: Two blocks are connected by a string. Block A (3 kg) sits on a frictionless table and is connected via a string over a pulley to Block B (2 kg) hanging vertically. What is the acceleration of the system? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².

hints.text: Treat the system as a whole. The only unbalanced force is the weight of the hanging block. Total mass = \(m_A + m_B\).

solution_steps.text: Net force driving the system: \(m_B g = 2(10) = 20\) N.

problems.question_html: If the net force on a 4 kg object is tripled while its mass is doubled, by what factor does the acceleration change?

hints.text: \(a = F/m\). If \(F \to 3F\) and \(m \to 2m\), what happens to \(a\)?

solution_steps.text: The acceleration increases by a factor of 1.5.

problems.question_html: A 1500 kg car experiences a 3000 N engine force and 1200 N friction force. What is the acceleration in m/s²?
A 70 kg person rides an elevator. The scale reads 560 N. Is the elevator accelerating up, down, or not at all? What is the acceleration? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².
problems.sample_answer: The person's weight is mg = 700 N, but the scale reads only 560 N. Since the apparent weight is less than the actual weight, the elevator accelerates downward. N - mg = ma: 560 - 700 = 70a → a = -2 m/s² (downward at 2 m/s²).
rubric: Correctly computes mg = 700 N and compares to scale reading of 560 N
Identifies that the elevator accelerates downward (apparent weight < actual weight)
Correctly computes a = 2 m/s² downward using Newton's Second Law

hints.text: Compare the scale reading to the person's weight (\(mg\)). If the reading is less than \(mg\), which direction is the acceleration?
\(mg = 700\) N > 560 N scale reading → acceleration is downward. \(560 - 700 = 70a \Rightarrow a = -2\) m/s².

solution_steps.text: Weight: \(mg = 70(10) = 700\) N. Scale reads 560 N < 700 N.
Since apparent weight < actual weight, the elevator accelerates downward.
\(N - mg = ma\): \(560 - 700 = 70a \Rightarrow a = -2\) m/s² (2 m/s² downward).

problems.correct_answer: The person's weight is mg = 700 N, but the scale reads only 560 N. Since the apparent weight is less than the actual weight, the elevator accelerates downward. N - mg = ma: 560 - 700 = 70a → a = -2 m/s² (downward at 2 m/s²).

concepts.title: Gravitational Force
concepts.content_html:
Gravitational Force

Every object in the universe attracts every other object. The force that keeps planets in orbit and apples falling from trees is the same: gravity.

Weight Near Earth's Surface

Near Earth's surface, the gravitational force on an object (its weight) is:

\[ F_g = mg \]

where \( g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 \approx 10 \text{ m/s}^2 \) is the gravitational field strength (acceleration due to gravity).

Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

The gravitational force between any two masses:

\[ F_g = \frac{Gm_1 m_2}{r^2} \]

where:

  • \( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \) — gravitational constant
  • \( m_1, m_2 \) — the two masses (kg)
  • \( r \) — distance between their centers (m)

Gravitational Field

The gravitational field strength at a distance \(r\) from mass \(M\) is:

\[ g = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

On Earth's surface, \( g = \frac{GM_E}{R_E^2} \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 \).

Key Idea: Gravitational force is always attractive, acts between any two masses, and follows an inverse-square law — double the distance and the force drops to one-quarter.
AP Exam Tip: The value of \(g\) varies with altitude and location. Near Earth's surface, use \(g = 9.8\) (or 10) m/s², but for objects far from Earth, use the universal law.

problems.question_html: What is the weight of a 70 kg person on Earth? Use \(g = 10\) m/s².
If the distance between two objects is tripled, by what factor does the gravitational force change?

hints.text: If \(r \to 3r\), then \(F \to F/(3^2) = F/9\). The force is one-ninth as strong.

solution_steps.text: The force decreases by a factor of 9.

problems.question_html: The Moon is about 60 Earth radii from Earth's center. What is the gravitational field strength at the Moon's distance, compared to Earth's surface? Express as a fraction of \(g\).

solution_steps.text: At the Moon's distance, \(g\) is only \(1/3600\) of its surface value.

problems.question_html: A 60 kg person weighs 600 N on Earth. What is their weight on a planet where \(g = 4\) m/s²? Give your answer in newtons.

hints.text: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength of the planet.

solution_steps.text: \(W = mg = 60 \times 4 = 240\) N. Mass stays the same; weight changes with \(g\).

problems.question_html: Two 50 kg masses are 2 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them? Use \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N·m²/kg².
If Earth's mass stayed the same but its radius shrank to half, what would happen to \(g\) at the surface?
Planet X has twice Earth's mass and twice Earth's radius. What is the surface gravitational field strength on Planet X, compared to Earth's \(g\)?

hints.text: \(g = GM/R^2\). If \(M \to 2M\) and \(R \to 2R\), how does \(g\) change?

solution_steps.text: Despite having twice the mass, the larger radius reduces \(g\) by a factor of 4, netting \(g/2\).

problems.question_html: Explain why astronauts on the International Space Station appear weightless even though gravity is about 90% of its surface value at that altitude.
problems.sample_answer: The ISS and astronauts are in free fall — they orbit Earth, continuously falling toward it while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it. Because both the station and astronauts fall at the same rate, there is no contact force between them (no normal force), creating the sensation of weightlessness. They are not beyond the reach of gravity.
rubric: Identifies that the ISS is in free fall / orbit (not beyond gravity's reach)
Explains that astronauts and station fall at the same rate
Connects the lack of normal force to the sensation of weightlessness

hints.text: The ISS orbits at about 400 km altitude. \(g\) there is about 8.7 m/s². So gravity is very much present.
The astronauts and the station are both in free fall — falling at the same rate. With no relative acceleration between them, there's no normal force, which creates the feeling of weightlessness.

solution_steps.text: At ISS altitude (~400 km), \(g \approx 8.7\) m/s² — only ~11% less than at the surface.
The ISS orbits Earth — it is continuously falling toward Earth while moving sideways.
Since the astronauts and station fall at the same rate, there is no normal force between them. This absence of contact force is what we perceive as weightlessness.

problems.correct_answer: The ISS and astronauts are in free fall — they orbit Earth, continuously falling toward it while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it. concepts.title: Kinetic and Static Friction
concepts.content_html:
Kinetic and Static Friction

Try pushing a heavy bookcase across the floor. At first it doesn't budge — static friction holds it. Push harder and it suddenly slides, now opposed by kinetic friction, which is generally less than the maximum static friction.

Static Friction

Static friction prevents an object from starting to move. It adjusts to match the applied force, up to a maximum:

\[ f_s \leq \mu_s F_N \]

The object begins to slide when the applied force exceeds \( \mu_s F_N \).

Kinetic Friction

Once sliding, kinetic friction acts on the object:

\[ f_k = \mu_k F_N \]

Kinetic friction is approximately constant and typically less than maximum static friction: \( \mu_k < \mu_s \).

Variable Definitions

  • \( f_s \) — static friction force (N)
  • \( f_k \) — kinetic friction force (N)
  • \( \mu_s \) — coefficient of static friction (dimensionless)
  • \( \mu_k \) — coefficient of kinetic friction (dimensionless)
  • \( F_N \) — normal force (N)

Direction of Friction

Friction always opposes the relative motion (kinetic) or the tendency of motion (static) between two surfaces.

Key Idea: Friction depends on the normal force, not the surface area. On an incline, the normal force is \(mg\cos\theta\), NOT \(mg\).
AP Exam Tip: Static friction is NOT always equal to \(\mu_s F_N\). That's the MAXIMUM value. Static friction can be any value from 0 up to \(\mu_s F_N\).

concepts.title: Spring Forces
concepts.content_html:
Spring Forces

When you stretch or compress a spring, it pushes back. The harder you pull, the harder it resists — and the relationship is remarkably simple.

Hooke's Law

The force exerted by a spring is proportional to its displacement from the natural (unstretched) length:

\[ F_s = -kx \]

The negative sign means the spring force is always a restoring force — it acts in the direction opposite to the displacement.

The magnitude of the spring force is:

\[ |F_s| = k|x| \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( F_s \) — spring force (N)
  • \( k \) — spring constant (N/m) — a measure of the spring's stiffness
  • \( x \) — displacement from natural length (m)

Spring Constant

A large \(k\) means a stiff spring (hard to stretch). A small \(k\) means a soft spring (easy to stretch).

\(k\) can be found experimentally by measuring the force needed to stretch the spring a known amount:

\[ k = \frac{F}{x} \]

Elastic Limit

Hooke's Law applies only within the elastic limit. If stretched too far, the spring deforms permanently and the linear relationship breaks down.

Key Idea: Hooke's Law is linear: double the displacement → double the force. The spring constant \(k\) is the slope of a force vs. displacement graph.
AP Exam Tip: Watch the sign convention. If the spring is compressed (\(x < 0\)), the force is positive (pushes outward). The restoring nature of the spring force is central to understanding oscillations (Unit 7).

concepts.title: Circular Motion
concepts.content_html:
Circular Motion

A car rounding a curve, a satellite orbiting Earth, a ball on a string — these all involve circular motion, where the direction of velocity is constantly changing.

Uniform Circular Motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed has:

  • Constant speed \(v\)
  • Changing velocity (direction changes)
  • Acceleration directed toward the center: centripetal acceleration

\[ a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} \]

Centripetal Force

By Newton's Second Law, the net force causing circular motion points toward the center:

\[ F_c = ma_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} \]

This is NOT a new type of force — it's the name for whatever real force (tension, gravity, friction, normal force) provides the inward acceleration.

Period and Frequency

\[ T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} \qquad f = \frac{1}{T} \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( a_c \) — centripetal acceleration (m/s²)
  • \( v \) — speed (m/s)
  • \( r \) — radius of circular path (m)
  • \( T \) — period (s) — time for one revolution
  • \( f \) — frequency (Hz) — revolutions per second
Key Idea: "Centripetal" means "center-seeking." There is no outward centripetal force on the object — the inward force is what keeps it moving in a circle. "Centrifugal force" is a fictitious force felt in a rotating reference frame.
AP Exam Tip: Never write "centripetal force" as a label on a free-body diagram. Instead, identify the real force (tension, gravity, friction, normal) that acts as the centripetal force.

concepts.title: Translational Kinetic Energy
concepts.content_html:
Translational Kinetic Energy

A moving truck carries more "punch" than a moving bicycle. Kinetic energy quantifies the energy an object has due to its motion.

Definition

The translational kinetic energy of an object with mass \(m\) moving at speed \(v\):

\[ K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \]

Key Properties

  • Kinetic energy is always positive (or zero)
  • It is a scalar — no direction
  • It depends on the square of speed: double the speed → quadruple the KE
  • SI unit: joule (J) = kg·m²/s²

Variable Definitions

  • \( K \) — kinetic energy (J)
  • \( m \) — mass (kg)
  • \( v \) — speed (m/s)
Key Idea: Because KE depends on \(v^2\), small changes in speed at high velocities produce large changes in kinetic energy. Going from 10 to 20 m/s triples the KE, not doubles it.
AP Exam Tip: Kinetic energy is frame-dependent — it depends on the observer's reference frame. The AP exam usually assumes the ground frame unless stated otherwise.

concepts.title: Work
concepts.content_html:
Work

In physics, "work" has a precise meaning: it's the transfer of energy to an object by a force acting on it through a displacement.

Work Done by a Constant Force

\[ W = Fd\cos\theta \]

where \(F\) is the magnitude of the force, \(d\) is the magnitude of the displacement, and \(\theta\) is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.

Special Cases

  • \(\theta = 0°\): force and displacement in same direction → \(W = Fd\) (positive work)
  • \(\theta = 90°\): force perpendicular to displacement → \(W = 0\) (no work)
  • \(\theta = 180°\): force opposite to displacement → \(W = -Fd\) (negative work)

Work-Energy Theorem

The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

\[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2 \]

Work Done by Variable Forces

For a force that changes, work equals the area under the force vs. displacement graph.

Variable Definitions

  • \( W \) — work (J)
  • \( F \) — force magnitude (N)
  • \( d \) — displacement magnitude (m)
  • \( \theta \) — angle between force and displacement
Key Idea: The normal force and gravity do zero work when an object moves horizontally, because they are perpendicular to the displacement. Work requires a force component along the direction of motion.
AP Exam Tip: Negative work doesn't mean "less" work — it means the force takes energy away from the object (e.g., friction slowing something down).

\(W = Fd\cos 90° = 0\) J. No energy is transferred by the carrying force.

concepts.title: Potential Energy
concepts.content_html:
Potential Energy

A book on a high shelf has energy stored in it — not because it's moving, but because of its position. This stored energy is potential energy.

Gravitational Potential Energy

Near Earth's surface:

\[ U_g = mgh \]

where \(h\) is the height above a chosen reference level. The reference level (where \(h = 0\)) is arbitrary — only changes in PE matter.

Elastic (Spring) Potential Energy

Energy stored in a compressed or stretched spring:

\[ U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 \]

where \(x\) is the displacement from the natural length.

Work Done by Conservative Forces

Gravity and spring forces are conservative: the work they do depends only on initial and final positions, not the path. For conservative forces:

\[ W_{\text{conservative}} = -\Delta U \]

Friction is non-conservative — the work it does depends on the path.

Variable Definitions

  • \( U_g \) — gravitational PE (J)
  • \( U_s \) — spring PE (J)
  • \( h \) — height above reference (m)
  • \( k \) — spring constant (N/m)
  • \( x \) — spring displacement (m)
Key Idea: Potential energy is energy of position or configuration. Only changes in PE are physically meaningful — the zero level is a matter of convenience.
AP Exam Tip: Choose your reference level wisely (usually the lowest point in the problem). Once chosen, be consistent throughout.

A 5 kg object falls from 10 m to 4 m. What is the change in gravitational PE? Use \(g = 10\) m/s². Give your answer in joules.

This matters because non-conservative forces convert mechanical energy into thermal energy (heat), so total mechanical energy is not conserved when friction is present.

concepts.title: Conservation of Energy
concepts.content_html:
Conservation of Energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transformed from one form to another. This principle is one of the most powerful problem-solving tools in physics.

Conservation of Mechanical Energy

When only conservative forces act (no friction, no air resistance):

\[ K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \]

or equivalently:

\[ \Delta K + \Delta U = 0 \]

With Non-Conservative Forces

When friction or other non-conservative forces are present:

\[ K_i + U_i + W_{\text{nc}} = K_f + U_f \]

where \(W_{\text{nc}}\) is the work done by non-conservative forces (usually negative for friction).

Equivalently: \(\Delta E_{\text{mech}} = W_{\text{nc}}\). Friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy.

Problem-Solving Strategy

  1. Define the system and identify initial and final states
  2. Choose a reference level for gravitational PE
  3. Identify all energy types present at each state
  4. Determine if non-conservative forces do work
  5. Apply the energy equation and solve
Key Idea: Energy conservation often avoids the need for force and acceleration analysis. If you only need to relate speeds and heights (not time or force), energy methods are usually simpler.
AP Exam Tip: The AP exam loves problems where energy conservation is simpler than kinematics — roller coasters, pendulums, objects on ramps. Always consider energy methods first.

concepts.title: Power
concepts.content_html:
Power

Two cars climb the same hill. One takes 10 seconds, the other takes 30 seconds. Both do the same work, but the faster car uses more power.

Definition

Power is the rate at which work is done (or energy is transferred):

\[ P = \frac{W}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t} \]

Instantaneous Power

For a constant force on an object moving at velocity \(v\):

\[ P = Fv\cos\theta \]

When force and velocity are in the same direction:

\[ P = Fv \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( P \) — power (W = J/s)
  • \( W \) — work (J)
  • \( \Delta t \) — time interval (s)
  • \( F \) — force (N)
  • \( v \) — velocity (m/s)

Units

SI unit: watt (W) = 1 J/s. Also: 1 horsepower (hp) ≈ 746 W.

Key Idea: Power doesn't tell you how much energy is transferred — it tells you how quickly. High power means the same work is done in less time.
AP Exam Tip: When a car moves at constant velocity against friction, the engine power equals \(P = fv\), where \(f\) is the friction force. This is because net force is zero at constant velocity.

problems.question_html: Two cars have the same mass. Car A has twice the power of Car B. Since W = Fd and both travel the same d with the engine force equal to P/v (varying), the analysis is complex. By W-E theorem, if the same work W is done (same F, same d), then Δ KE is the same regardless of power. So both cars reach the same speed after the same distance — power only affects HOW QUICKLY they reach that speed.

Explains that power affects time to reach that speed, not the speed itself at a given distance

If the net force is the same and the distance is the same, the work done is the same — so the final KE (and speed) is the same. Power determines how fast this happens, not the final speed.

If the same net force acts over the same distance, the work (and thus final speed) is identical.
Power determines the rate of energy transfer — Car A reaches the final speed in less time, but both reach the same speed after the same distance.

concepts.title: Linear Momentum
concepts.content_html:
Linear Momentum

A slow-moving freight train is hard to stop, and so is a speeding bullet — but for different reasons. Momentum captures both mass and velocity in one quantity.

Definition

The linear momentum of an object is:

\[ \vec{p} = m\vec{v} \]

Properties

  • Momentum is a vector — it has the same direction as velocity
  • SI unit: kg·m/s
  • A heavy slow object can have the same momentum as a light fast object

Momentum of a System

The total momentum of a system is the vector sum of all individual momenta:

\[ \vec{p}_{\text{total}} = \sum m_i \vec{v}_i \]

Key Idea: Momentum is a vector — direction matters. Two objects moving in opposite directions can have zero total momentum even though both are moving.
AP Exam Tip: Don't confuse momentum (\(p = mv\)) with kinetic energy (\(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\)). They are different quantities and not interchangeable.

concepts.title: Change in Momentum and Impulse
concepts.content_html:
Change in Momentum and Impulse

A tennis racket striking a ball exerts a large force over a short time. The result — a change in the ball's momentum — is called impulse.

Impulse-Momentum Theorem

The impulse delivered to an object equals its change in momentum:

\[ \vec{J} = \vec{F}_{\text{avg}} \Delta t = \Delta \vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i \]

Force-Time Graphs

Impulse equals the area under a force vs. time graph. For a variable force, integrate the area.

Reducing Impact Force

Since \(J = F\Delta t\) is fixed for a given momentum change, increasing the time of impact decreases the force:

  • Airbags increase collision time → reduce force on passengers
  • Catching a ball by "giving" with your hand → longer contact time → less force
Key Idea: Impulse is the bridge between force (Newton's Second Law) and momentum. \(\vec{F} = \frac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}\) is actually Newton's original formulation of the Second Law.
AP Exam Tip: When a ball bounces off a wall, the change in momentum is larger than if it sticks (because the velocity reverses direction). Don't forget to account for the sign change.

concepts.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
concepts.content_html:
Conservation of Linear Momentum

When two ice skaters push off each other, one goes left and the other goes right — but the total momentum of the system stays the same: zero.

The Law

If the net external force on a system is zero, the total momentum of the system is conserved:

\[ \vec{p}_i = \vec{p}_f \]

\[ m_1 \vec{v}_{1i} + m_2 \vec{v}_{2i} = m_1 \vec{v}_{1f} + m_2 \vec{v}_{2f} \]

When Is Momentum Conserved?

Momentum is conserved when:

  • No net external force acts on the system
  • Or the external forces are negligible compared to internal forces (e.g., during a brief collision, gravity is negligible)

Types of Events

  • Collisions: objects come together (momentum always conserved)
  • Explosions: one object splits into pieces (momentum conserved)
Key Idea: Momentum conservation applies to the SYSTEM, not individual objects. Each object's momentum changes, but the total stays constant.
AP Exam Tip: In 2D problems, apply conservation of momentum separately in x and y directions. Momentum is a vector — you must conserve each component.

concepts.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
concepts.content_html:
Elastic and Inelastic Collisions

When two billiard balls collide, they bounce apart and the total kinetic energy is nearly the same before and after. When two lumps of clay collide, they stick together and kinetic energy is lost. These represent different types of collisions.

Types of Collisions

  • Perfectly elastic: momentum AND kinetic energy are both conserved. Objects bounce apart. (Ideal case — atom-atom collisions, billiards approximately)
  • Perfectly inelastic: momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is NOT. Objects stick together. Maximum KE loss.
  • Inelastic: momentum is conserved, some KE is lost (but not maximum). Most real collisions.

Perfectly Inelastic (Stick Together)

\[ m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i} = (m_1 + m_2) v_f \]

Elastic Collision (1D, object 2 at rest)

\[ v_{1f} = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2} v_{1i} \qquad v_{2f} = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2} v_{1i} \]

KE Lost in Inelastic Collisions

\[ \Delta K = K_f - K_i \]

This "lost" KE is converted to thermal energy, sound, and deformation.

Key Idea: Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in collisions (both elastic and inelastic). Kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions.
AP Exam Tip: To determine if a collision is elastic, compute the total KE before and after. If they're equal, it's elastic. If not, it's inelastic. You don't need to memorize the elastic collision formulas — they're derived from conservation of momentum + conservation of KE.

concepts.title: Rotational Kinematics
concepts.content_html:
A spinning figure skater, a rotating Ferris wheel, a turning bicycle tire — rotational motion is everywhere. Just as we described translational motion with position, velocity, and acceleration, we can describe rotation with analogous quantities.

Angular Position and Displacement

Angular position \( \theta \) measures how far an object has rotated from a reference line, in radians (rad).

\[ \Delta\theta = \theta_f - \theta_i \]

Angular displacement \( \Delta\theta \) is the change in angular position. A full revolution equals \( 2\pi \) rad (360°).

Angular Velocity

Angular velocity \( \omega \) is the rate of change of angular position:

\[ \omega = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} \]

Units: rad/s. Positive \( \omega \) indicates counterclockwise rotation (by convention).

Angular Acceleration

Angular acceleration \( \alpha \) is the rate of change of angular velocity:

\[ \alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t} \]

Units: rad/s². When \( \alpha \) has the same sign as \( \omega \), the object speeds up rotationally; opposite signs mean it slows down.

Rotational Kinematic Equations

For constant angular acceleration, the kinematic equations mirror their translational counterparts:

\[ \omega_f = \omega_i + \alpha t \]

\[ \Delta\theta = \omega_i t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 \]

\[ \omega_f^2 = \omega_i^2 + 2\alpha\,\Delta\theta \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( \theta \) = angular position (rad)
  • \( \omega \) = angular velocity (rad/s)
  • \( \alpha \) = angular acceleration (rad/s²)
  • \( t \) = time (s)

Worked Example

A wheel starts from rest and accelerates at \( \alpha = 4.0 \) rad/s² for 3.0 s. Find the angular displacement.

\[ \Delta\theta = \omega_i t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(4.0)(3.0)^2 = 18 \text{ rad} \]

That's \( 18 / (2\pi) \approx 2.9 \) revolutions.

Key Idea: Rotational kinematic equations have the exact same structure as translational kinematics — just replace \( x \) with \( \theta \), \( v \) with \( \omega \), and \( a \) with \( \alpha \).
AP Exam Tip: Always use radians (not degrees) in rotational calculations. The kinematic equations only work with radian measure.

concepts.title: Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion
concepts.content_html:
A point on the rim of a spinning bicycle wheel moves in a circle. It has both a linear (tangential) velocity and an angular velocity. How are these related?

Arc Length and Angular Displacement

For a point at distance \( r \) from the axis of rotation:

\[ s = r\,\Delta\theta \]

where \( s \) is the arc length traveled and \( \Delta\theta \) is in radians.

Tangential Velocity

The tangential velocity (or linear speed) of a point on a rotating object is:

\[ v = r\omega \]

Points farther from the axis move faster, even though all points share the same \( \omega \).

Tangential Acceleration

If the angular velocity changes, there is a tangential acceleration:

\[ a_t = r\alpha \]

Centripetal Acceleration

Any point undergoing circular motion also has centripetal acceleration directed toward the center:

\[ a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = r\omega^2 \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( s \) = arc length (m)
  • \( r \) = radius / distance from axis (m)
  • \( v \) = tangential speed (m/s)
  • \( a_t \) = tangential acceleration (m/s²)
  • \( a_c \) = centripetal acceleration (m/s²)

Worked Example

A wheel of radius \( 0.30 \) m spins at \( 20 \) rad/s. What is the linear speed of a point on the rim?

\[ v = r\omega = (0.30)(20) = 6.0 \text{ m/s} \]

Key Idea: All points on a rigid rotating object share the same \( \omega \) and \( \alpha \), but points farther from the axis have greater linear speed and tangential acceleration.
AP Exam Tip: Don't confuse tangential acceleration (changes speed) with centripetal acceleration (changes direction). A point on a uniformly spinning wheel has centripetal acceleration but zero tangential acceleration.

problems.question_html: A disk accelerates uniformly from rest. Explain why a point on the outer edge of the disk experiences both tangential and centripetal acceleration, and describe how the direction and magnitude of each component change over time.

concepts.title: Torque
concepts.content_html:
Opening a door, tightening a bolt with a wrench, or turning a steering wheel — all involve torque. Torque is the rotational equivalent of force: it causes angular acceleration.

Definition of Torque

Torque \( \tau \) measures the tendency of a force to cause rotation about a pivot point (axis of rotation):

\[ \tau = rF\sin\theta \]

where \( r \) is the distance from the pivot to where the force is applied, \( F \) is the magnitude of the force, and \( \theta \) is the angle between \( \vec{r} \) and \( \vec{F} \).

Lever Arm

The lever arm (or moment arm) \( r_{\perp} \) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force:

\[ \tau = r_{\perp} F = rF\sin\theta \]

Maximum torque occurs when the force is perpendicular to \( \vec{r} \) (\( \theta = 90° \)), so \( \tau = rF \).

Sign Convention

Torques causing counterclockwise rotation are positive; clockwise torques are negative.

Net Torque

The net torque on an object is the sum of all individual torques about the same pivot:

\[ \sum\tau = \tau_1 + \tau_2 + \cdots \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( \tau \) = torque (N·m)
  • \( r \) = distance from pivot to point of force application (m)
  • \( F \) = force magnitude (N)
  • \( \theta \) = angle between \( \vec{r} \) and \( \vec{F} \)
  • \( r_{\perp} \) = lever arm / moment arm (m)

Worked Example

You push on a door \( 0.80 \) m from the hinge with a force of \( 25 \) N perpendicular to the door. What is the torque?

\[ \tau = rF\sin 90° = (0.80)(25)(1) = 20 \text{ N·m} \]

Key Idea: Torque depends on three things: how much force, how far from the pivot, and the angle. Pushing at the edge of a door (large \( r \)) is much easier than pushing near the hinge (small \( r \)).
AP Exam Tip: When \( \theta = 0° \) or \( 180° \), the torque is zero — the force acts along the line from the pivot and cannot cause rotation. Always identify the angle carefully.

Two forces act on a beam pivoted at its center. Force \( F_1 = 30 \) N acts downward at \( 0.40 \) m to the left of the pivot. Force \( F_2 = 20 \) N acts downward at \( 0.60 \) m to the right. What is the net torque about the pivot?

solution_steps.text: \( F_1 \) acts left of pivot, pulling down → counterclockwise: \( \tau_1 = +(0.40)(30) = +12 \) N·m.
\( F_2 \) acts right of pivot, pulling down → clockwise: \( \tau_2 = -(0.60)(20) = -12 \) N·m.
Net torque = \( 12 + (-12) = 0 \) N·m. The beam is balanced.

concepts.title: Rotational Inertia
concepts.content_html:
Why is it harder to spin a long barbell than a compact dumbbell of the same mass? The answer lies in rotational inertia — the rotational analog of mass.

Definition

Rotational inertia (also called moment of inertia) \( I \) quantifies an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion. For a collection of point masses:

\[ I = \sum m_i r_i^2 \]

where \( m_i \) is the mass of each particle and \( r_i \) is its distance from the axis of rotation.

Key Dependence

Rotational inertia depends on:

  1. Total mass — more mass means more rotational inertia
  2. Distribution of mass — mass farther from the axis contributes more (quadratically)
  3. Choice of axis — the same object has different \( I \) values for different rotation axes

Common Shapes (Given on AP Exam)

  • Solid cylinder/disk: \( I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 \)
  • Hollow cylinder (thin ring): \( I = MR^2 \)
  • Solid sphere: \( I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 \)
  • Hollow sphere: \( I = \frac{2}{3}MR^2 \)
  • Thin rod about center: \( I = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 \)
  • Thin rod about end: \( I = \frac{1}{3}ML^2 \)

Variable Definitions

  • \( I \) = rotational inertia / moment of inertia (kg·m²)
  • \( m_i \) = mass of individual particle (kg)
  • \( r_i \) = distance of particle from axis (m)
  • \( M \) = total mass (kg)
  • \( R \) = radius (m)

Worked Example

Two masses of \( 2.0 \) kg each are attached to the ends of a \( 0.50 \) m rod (of negligible mass). What is the rotational inertia about the center of the rod?

Each mass is \( r = 0.25 \) m from the center:

\[ I = \sum m_i r_i^2 = 2.0(0.25)^2 + 2.0(0.25)^2 = 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.25 \text{ kg·m²} \]

Key Idea: Rotational inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis. Moving mass farther from the axis increases \( I \) dramatically because distance is squared.
AP Exam Tip: The AP exam provides formulas for common shapes. You don't need to memorize them, but you must know how to apply them and compare objects by their mass distribution.

problems.question_html: Two solid cylinders have the same mass \( M \). Cylinder A has radius \( R \) and cylinder B has radius \( 2R \). Explain how their rotational inertias compare and why mass distribution matters for rotation.
