concepts.title: Rotational Equilibrium and Newton's First Law in Rotational Form
concepts.content_html:
A balanced seesaw, a hanging sign that doesn't rotate, a bridge that remains level — these are all examples of rotational equilibrium.

Newton's First Law for Rotation

An object in rotational equilibrium has zero net torque and therefore zero angular acceleration. It either remains at rest (not rotating) or rotates at constant angular velocity:

\[ \sum\tau = 0 \implies \alpha = 0 \]

Static Equilibrium

An object in static equilibrium satisfies two conditions simultaneously:

  1. Translational: \( \sum\vec{F} = 0 \) (no net force)
  2. Rotational: \( \sum\tau = 0 \) (no net torque about any point)

Choosing a Pivot Point

For equilibrium problems, you can choose any point as the pivot for calculating torques. A smart choice eliminates unknown forces from the torque equation. Often, choosing the point where an unknown force acts is the best strategy.

Solving Static Equilibrium Problems

  1. Draw a free-body diagram showing all forces and where they act
  2. Set \( \sum F_x = 0 \) and \( \sum F_y = 0 \)
  3. Choose a convenient pivot and set \( \sum\tau = 0 \)
  4. Solve the system of equations

Worked Example

A \( 4.0 \) m uniform beam (weight \( 200 \) N) rests on two supports: one at each end. A \( 300 \) N person stands \( 1.0 \) m from the left end. Find the force at each support.

Choose left support as pivot:

\[ \sum\tau = 0: \quad (300)(1.0) + (200)(2.0) - F_R(4.0) = 0 \]

\[ 300 + 400 = 4.0\,F_R \implies F_R = 175 \text{ N} \]

From \( \sum F_y = 0 \): \( F_L = 200 + 300 - 175 = 325 \) N.

concepts.title: Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form
concepts.content_html:
Just as \( F = ma \) connects force to translational acceleration, there is a rotational version that connects torque to angular acceleration.

Newton's Second Law for Rotation

\[ \sum\tau = I\alpha \]

The net torque on an object equals its rotational inertia times its angular acceleration. This is the fundamental equation of rotational dynamics.

Analogy to Translation

TranslationRotation
\( F \) (force)\( \tau \) (torque)
\( m \) (mass)\( I \) (rotational inertia)
\( a \) (acceleration)\( \alpha \) (angular acceleration)
\( F = ma \)\( \tau = I\alpha \)

Problem-Solving Strategy

  1. Identify the axis of rotation
  2. Draw free-body diagrams showing where forces act
  3. Calculate each torque about the axis
  4. Find or calculate \( I \) for the object
  5. Apply \( \sum\tau = I\alpha \) to find \( \alpha \)

Variable Definitions

  • \( \sum\tau \) = net torque (N·m)
  • \( I \) = rotational inertia (kg·m²)
  • \( \alpha \) = angular acceleration (rad/s²)

Worked Example

A solid disk of mass \( 4.0 \) kg and radius \( 0.20 \) m has a tangential force of \( 10 \) N applied at its rim. What is the angular acceleration?

\[ I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(4.0)(0.20)^2 = 0.080 \text{ kg·m²} \]

\[ \tau = FR = (10)(0.20) = 2.0 \text{ N·m} \]

\[ \alpha = \frac{\tau}{I} = \frac{2.0}{0.080} = 25 \text{ rad/s²} \]

Key Idea: \( \tau = I\alpha \) is the rotational analog of \( F = ma \). A larger rotational inertia means the same torque produces a smaller angular acceleration.
AP Exam Tip: Many problems combine translational and rotational dynamics (e.g., a block connected to a pulley by a string). Set up \( F = ma \) for the translating object and \( \tau = I\alpha \) for the rotating object, then use the constraint \( a = R\alpha \) to connect them.

concepts.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
concepts.content_html:
A spinning flywheel stores energy. A rotating merry-go-round can do work if it slows down. This energy of rotation is called rotational kinetic energy.

Definition

\[ K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 \]

This is the rotational analog of translational kinetic energy \( K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \).

Total Kinetic Energy

An object that both translates and rotates (like a rolling ball) has total kinetic energy:

\[ K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 \]

where \( v_{\text{cm}} \) is the speed of the center of mass.

Variable Definitions

  • \( K_{\text{rot}} \) = rotational kinetic energy (J)
  • \( I \) = rotational inertia (kg·m²)
  • \( \omega \) = angular velocity (rad/s)
  • \( v_{\text{cm}} \) = center-of-mass velocity (m/s)

Worked Example

A solid disk of mass \( 3.0 \) kg and radius \( 0.20 \) m spins at \( 10 \) rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy?

\[ I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(3.0)(0.20)^2 = 0.060 \text{ kg·m²} \]

\[ K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.060)(10)^2 = 3.0 \text{ J} \]

Key Idea: Rotational kinetic energy depends on both how much rotational inertia an object has and how fast it spins. Doubling \( \omega \) quadruples the energy.
AP Exam Tip: When applying conservation of energy to rolling objects, you must include both translational AND rotational kinetic energy. Forgetting the rotational term is a common error.

Solving: v = √(4gh/3). A sliding box has no rotational KE, so mgh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gh). Since √(4gh/3) < √(2gh), the rolling cylinder is slower. This is because some gravitational PE goes into rotational KE instead of all going into translational KE.

concepts.title: Torque and Work
concepts.content_html:
Just as a force does work when it moves an object through a displacement, a torque does work when it rotates an object through an angular displacement.

Work Done by Torque

\[ W = \tau\,\Delta\theta \]

where \( \tau \) is the constant torque and \( \Delta\theta \) is the angular displacement in radians. This is the rotational analog of \( W = Fd \).

Work-Energy Theorem for Rotation

The net work done on a rotating object equals the change in its rotational kinetic energy:

\[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}I\omega_i^2 \]

Power in Rotation

Rotational power is the rate of doing rotational work:

\[ P = \tau\omega \]

This is analogous to \( P = Fv \).

Variable Definitions

  • \( W \) = work (J)
  • \( \tau \) = torque (N·m)
  • \( \Delta\theta \) = angular displacement (rad)
  • \( P \) = power (W)

Worked Example

A constant torque of \( 6.0 \) N·m spins a wheel through \( 10 \) rad. How much work is done?

\[ W = \tau\,\Delta\theta = (6.0)(10) = 60 \text{ J} \]

Key Idea: Work done by torque follows the same pattern as translational work — just swap force for torque and distance for angle.
AP Exam Tip: The angular displacement must be in radians for \( W = \tau\Delta\theta \) to give the answer in joules. Convert revolutions to radians if needed.

concepts.title: Angular Momentum and Angular Impulse
concepts.content_html:
A spinning top resists being tipped over. A gyroscope maintains its orientation. These effects arise from angular momentum — the rotational equivalent of linear momentum.

Angular Momentum

For a rigid object rotating about a fixed axis:

\[ L = I\omega \]

Angular momentum is a vector quantity. Its direction is along the axis of rotation (use the right-hand rule: curl fingers in the direction of rotation, thumb points in the direction of \( \vec{L} \)).

Angular Impulse

Just as impulse changes linear momentum, angular impulse changes angular momentum:

\[ \tau\,\Delta t = \Delta L = I\omega_f - I\omega_i \]

This is Newton's second law for rotation in impulse-momentum form.

Variable Definitions

  • \( L \) = angular momentum (kg·m²/s)
  • \( I \) = rotational inertia (kg·m²)
  • \( \omega \) = angular velocity (rad/s)
  • \( \tau \) = torque (N·m)
  • \( \Delta t \) = time interval (s)

Worked Example

A disk with \( I = 0.50 \) kg·m² spins at \( 20 \) rad/s. What is its angular momentum?

\[ L = I\omega = (0.50)(20) = 10 \text{ kg·m²/s} \]

If a braking torque of \( 2.0 \) N·m is applied, how long does it take to stop?

\[ \tau\,\Delta t = \Delta L \implies (2.0)\Delta t = 10 \implies \Delta t = 5.0 \text{ s} \]

Key Idea: Angular momentum \( L = I\omega \) is the rotational analog of linear momentum \( p = mv \). Angular impulse \( \tau\Delta t \) changes angular momentum just as \( F\Delta t \) changes linear momentum.
AP Exam Tip: Pay attention to the sign of angular momentum. If two objects rotate in opposite directions, their angular momenta have opposite signs and partially cancel when combined.

concepts.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
concepts.content_html:
When a figure skater pulls in her arms and spins faster, or when a diver tucks to flip more rapidly, angular momentum is being conserved. This principle is one of the most powerful in physics.

Conservation Law

When the net external torque on a system is zero, the total angular momentum is conserved:

\[ L_i = L_f \]

\[ I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f \]

Applications

  • Changing shape: A skater pulls arms in → \( I \) decreases → \( \omega \) increases (and vice versa)
  • Collisions: Two rotating objects that stick together conserve total angular momentum
  • Orbital motion: A planet closer to the sun moves faster because \( L \) is conserved

Important Note on Energy

When \( I \) changes, angular momentum is conserved but kinetic energy generally is NOT. Pulling arms in increases KE (internal energy from muscles converts to kinetic energy).

Variable Definitions

  • \( L \) = angular momentum (kg·m²/s)
  • \( I_i, I_f \) = initial and final rotational inertia (kg·m²)
  • \( \omega_i, \omega_f \) = initial and final angular velocity (rad/s)

Worked Example

A skater with \( I = 4.0 \) kg·m² spins at \( 3.0 \) rad/s. She pulls her arms in, reducing \( I \) to \( 1.5 \) kg·m². What is her new angular velocity?

\[ I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f \]

\[ (4.0)(3.0) = (1.5)\omega_f \implies \omega_f = 8.0 \text{ rad/s} \]

Key Idea: If no external torque acts, angular momentum is conserved. When rotational inertia decreases, angular velocity must increase to keep \( L = I\omega \) constant.
AP Exam Tip: Angular momentum conservation does NOT mean energy is conserved. When a skater pulls her arms in, she does internal work — her KE increases even though \( L \) stays the same.

concepts.title: Rolling
concepts.content_html:
A ball rolling down a hill, a tire moving along a road, a bowling ball on a lane — rolling is a combination of translation and rotation that appears everywhere in everyday life.

Rolling Without Slipping

When an object rolls without slipping, the contact point is momentarily at rest relative to the surface. This gives the key constraint:

\[ v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega \]

The center-of-mass speed equals the radius times the angular velocity. Differentiating:

\[ a_{\text{cm}} = R\alpha \]

Energy of Rolling

A rolling object has both translational and rotational kinetic energy:

\[ K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 \]

Using \( \omega = v/R \), this can be written as:

\[ K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1 + \frac{I}{mR^2}\right) \]

Rolling Down an Incline

For an object rolling down a frictionless ramp of height \( h \):

\[ mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 \]

Objects with smaller \( I/(mR^2) \) reach the bottom faster because more energy goes to translation.

Role of Friction

Static friction provides the torque needed for rolling without slipping. It does NOT do work (no displacement at the contact point). Without friction, the object would slide instead of roll.

Variable Definitions

  • \( v_{\text{cm}} \) = center-of-mass velocity (m/s)
  • \( R \) = radius (m)
  • \( \omega \) = angular velocity (rad/s)

Worked Example

A solid sphere and a hollow sphere of equal mass and radius roll down the same ramp. Which reaches the bottom first?

Solid sphere: \( I = \frac{2}{5}mR^2 \) → \( v = \sqrt{\frac{10gh}{7}} \)

Hollow sphere: \( I = \frac{2}{3}mR^2 \) → \( v = \sqrt{\frac{6gh}{5}} \)

Since \( \frac{10}{7} > \frac{6}{5} \), the solid sphere is faster. Less of its energy goes to rotation.

Key Idea: For rolling without slipping, \( v = R\omega \). Objects with lower \( I/(mR^2) \) ratios roll faster down inclines because a greater fraction of their energy is translational.
AP Exam Tip: Static friction is essential for rolling without slipping — it provides the torque — but it does no work. The energy analysis uses conservation of energy without a friction work term.

concepts.title: Motion of Orbiting Satellites
concepts.content_html:
The International Space Station orbits Earth every 90 minutes. The Moon takes about 27 days. Understanding orbital motion connects Newton's law of gravitation with circular motion and energy conservation.

Circular Orbits

For a satellite in a circular orbit, gravitational force provides the centripetal force:

\[ \frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r} \]

Solving for the orbital speed:

\[ v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \]

Key insight: orbital speed depends only on \( M \) (the central body's mass) and \( r \) (the orbital radius), NOT on the satellite's mass.

Orbital Period

The period of a circular orbit (time for one revolution):

\[ T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi r\sqrt{\frac{r}{GM}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}} \]

Gravitational Potential Energy

\[ U_g = -\frac{GMm}{r} \]

The negative sign means the object is bound. At \( r = \infty \), \( U = 0 \).

Total Energy in Orbit

\[ E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r} \]

The total energy is negative (bound orbit) and equals half the potential energy.

Variable Definitions

  • \( G \) = gravitational constant (\( 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \) N·m²/kg²)
  • \( M \) = mass of central body (kg)
  • \( m \) = mass of satellite (kg)
  • \( r \) = orbital radius from center of central body (m)
  • \( v \) = orbital speed (m/s)
  • \( T \) = orbital period (s)

Worked Example

A satellite orbits Earth at twice the radius of the ISS. How does its speed compare?

Since \( v \propto 1/\sqrt{r} \), doubling \( r \) gives \( v_{\text{new}} = v_{\text{ISS}} / \sqrt{2} \approx 0.71\,v_{\text{ISS}} \).

Key Idea: Higher orbits are slower. This seems counterintuitive, but increasing \( r \) weakens gravity, which means less centripetal force and thus a lower orbital speed.
AP Exam Tip: Don't confuse orbital radius \( r \) with altitude \( h \). The orbital radius is \( r = R_{\text{planet}} + h \), measured from the center of the planet, not the surface.

concepts.title: Defining Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
concepts.content_html:
A child on a swing, a vibrating guitar string, a mass bouncing on a spring — these are all examples of oscillatory motion. The simplest and most important type is simple harmonic motion (SHM).

What Is SHM?

Simple harmonic motion occurs when an object oscillates about an equilibrium position under the influence of a restoring force that is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium:

\[ F = -kx \]

The negative sign means the force always points back toward equilibrium. The constant \( k \) is the force constant (or spring constant for a spring system).

Characteristics of SHM

  • Amplitude \( A \): maximum displacement from equilibrium
  • Period \( T \): time for one complete cycle
  • Frequency \( f \): number of cycles per second (\( f = 1/T \))
  • Equilibrium position: the position where the net force is zero

Examples of SHM Systems

  • Mass-spring system: A mass on a spring oscillates horizontally or vertically
  • Simple pendulum: For small angles, a pendulum undergoes approximately SHM

Variable Definitions

  • \( F \) = restoring force (N)
  • \( k \) = spring/force constant (N/m)
  • \( x \) = displacement from equilibrium (m)
  • \( A \) = amplitude (m)
  • \( T \) = period (s)
  • \( f \) = frequency (Hz = 1/s)

Worked Example

A \( 0.50 \) kg mass on a spring (\( k = 20 \) N/m) is pulled \( 0.10 \) m from equilibrium and released. What is the restoring force at maximum displacement?

\[ F = -kx = -(20)(0.10) = -2.0 \text{ N} \]

The force is \( 2.0 \) N directed back toward equilibrium.

Key Idea: SHM requires a restoring force proportional to displacement. At equilibrium, the force (and acceleration) are zero but velocity is maximum. At maximum displacement, force and acceleration are maximum but velocity is zero.
AP Exam Tip: SHM is only exact when the restoring force is linear (\( F \propto x \)). A pendulum is approximately SHM only for small angles (roughly \( < 15° \)).

problems.question_html: Explain why a pendulum undergoes approximately simple harmonic motion only for small angles. What happens to the restoring force at large angles?
problems.sample_answer: For a pendulum, the restoring force component is F = −mg sin θ. For SHM, the force must be proportional to the displacement. When θ is small (in radians), sin θ ≈ θ, so F ≈ −mgθ, which is proportional to angular displacement — this is SHM. At large angles, sin θ is no longer approximately equal to θ (e.g., sin 30° = 0.50 but 30° = 0.524 rad). The restoring force is no longer proportional to displacement, and the motion deviates from SHM — the period increases with amplitude.

concepts.title: Frequency and Period of SHM
concepts.content_html:
How fast does a pendulum swing? How quickly does a mass on a spring bounce? The period and frequency of SHM depend on the physical properties of the system.

Mass-Spring System

\[ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} \qquad f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \]

The period depends on mass \( m \) and spring constant \( k \). It does not depend on amplitude.

Simple Pendulum

\[ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \qquad f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}} \]

The period depends on length \( L \) and gravitational acceleration \( g \). It does not depend on mass or amplitude (for small oscillations).

Angular Frequency

\[ \omega = 2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{T} \]

Angular frequency \( \omega \) has units of rad/s.

Variable Definitions

  • \( T \) = period (s)
  • \( f \) = frequency (Hz)
  • \( m \) = mass (kg)
  • \( k \) = spring constant (N/m)
  • \( L \) = pendulum length (m)
  • \( g \) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
  • \( \omega \) = angular frequency (rad/s)

Worked Example

A \( 0.50 \) kg mass hangs from a spring with \( k = 200 \) N/m. What is the period?

\[ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.50}{200}} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.0025} = 2\pi(0.050) = 0.31 \text{ s} \]

Key Idea: The period of SHM is independent of amplitude. A pendulum with a small swing takes the same time per cycle as one with a slightly larger swing. This is what makes pendulum clocks work.
AP Exam Tip: Don't confuse which formula goes with which system. Spring period depends on mass (not length); pendulum period depends on length (not mass). Both are independent of amplitude.

concepts.title: Representing and Analyzing SHM
concepts.content_html:
SHM can be described mathematically and graphically. Understanding the relationships between position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time is essential.

Position as a Function of Time

\[ x(t) = A\cos(\omega t) \]

(if starting from maximum displacement). Here \( \omega = 2\pi/T \) is the angular frequency.

Velocity

\[ v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t) \]

Maximum speed: \( v_{\text{max}} = A\omega \)

Acceleration

\[ a(t) = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 x \]

Maximum acceleration: \( a_{\text{max}} = A\omega^2 \)

Phase Relationships

  • Position and acceleration are 180° out of phase (when \( x \) is max positive, \( a \) is max negative)
  • Velocity is 90° ahead of position (velocity leads position by a quarter cycle)
  • When \( x = 0 \): \( |v| = v_{\text{max}} \), \( a = 0 \)
  • When \( |x| = A \): \( v = 0 \), \( |a| = a_{\text{max}} \)

Graphs

Position: cosine wave. Velocity: negative sine wave (shifted ¼ period left). Acceleration: negative cosine (shifted ½ period, i.e., inverted position graph).

Variable Definitions

  • \( A \) = amplitude (m)
  • \( \omega \) = angular frequency (rad/s)
  • \( v_{\text{max}} = A\omega \) = maximum speed (m/s)
  • \( a_{\text{max}} = A\omega^2 \) = maximum acceleration (m/s²)

Worked Example

A mass oscillates with \( A = 0.10 \) m and \( T = 0.50 \) s. Find the maximum speed.

\[ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{0.50} = 4\pi \text{ rad/s} \]

\[ v_{\text{max}} = A\omega = (0.10)(4\pi) = 0.40\pi \approx 1.26 \text{ m/s} \]

Key Idea: In SHM, acceleration is always opposite to displacement (\( a = -\omega^2 x \)). Position and velocity are 90° out of phase — velocity is zero at the extremes and maximum at equilibrium.
AP Exam Tip: On position-time graph questions, remember that the slope of \( x(t) \) gives velocity and the slope of \( v(t) \) gives acceleration. Check the graph at key points to match with physical behavior.

Acceleration a(t) is the derivative of velocity: a negative cosine, which is position inverted (180° out of phase). Velocity and acceleration are NEVER both zero at the same time — when v = 0 (at x = ±A), a is at maximum magnitude, and when a = 0 (at x = 0), v is at maximum magnitude. They can never both be at maximum magnitude simultaneously either: v_max occurs at x = 0 (where a = 0) and a_max occurs at x = ±A (where v = 0). Velocity and acceleration are 90° out of phase with each other.

solution_steps.text: \( x = A\cos(\omega t) \), \( v = -A\omega\sin(\omega t) \), \( a = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t) \).
\( v = 0 \) when \( \sin = 0 \) (at \( t = 0, T/2 \)). At these times, \( a = \mp A\omega^2 \) (maximum magnitude).
\( a = 0 \) when \( \cos = 0 \) (at \( t = T/4, 3T/4 \)). At these times, \( v = \mp A\omega \) (maximum magnitude).
So \( v \) and \( a \) are never both zero or both at maximum simultaneously — they are 90° out of phase.

concepts.title: Energy of Simple Harmonic Oscillators
concepts.content_html:
Energy sloshes back and forth between kinetic and potential forms in SHM. Understanding this energy exchange is key to analyzing oscillating systems.

Energy in a Mass-Spring System

Potential energy (stored in spring):

\[ U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 \]

Kinetic energy:

\[ K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \]

Total mechanical energy (constant, if no friction):

\[ E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \text{constant} \]

Energy at Key Positions

  • At \( x = \pm A \) (extremes): \( U = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \), \( K = 0 \) → all PE
  • At \( x = 0 \) (equilibrium): \( U = 0 \), \( K = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \) → all KE
  • At any position: \( K + U = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \)

Finding Speed at Any Position

From energy conservation:

\[ \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \]

\[ v = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}(A^2 - x^2)} = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( E \) = total mechanical energy (J)
  • \( U \) = elastic potential energy (J)
  • \( K \) = kinetic energy (J)
  • \( A \) = amplitude (m)
  • \( k \) = spring constant (N/m)

Worked Example

A \( 0.50 \) kg mass oscillates on a spring (\( k = 80 \) N/m) with amplitude \( 0.10 \) m. Find the speed when \( x = 0.060 \) m.

\[ v = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}(A^2 - x^2)} = \sqrt{\frac{80}{0.50}((0.10)^2 - (0.060)^2)} \]

\[ v = \sqrt{160(0.01 - 0.0036)} = \sqrt{160(0.0064)} = \sqrt{1.024} \approx 1.01 \text{ m/s} \]

Key Idea: Total energy in SHM is constant and proportional to \( A^2 \). Doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy. Energy continuously transforms between kinetic and potential forms.
AP Exam Tip: Energy conservation gives you a powerful shortcut. Instead of using kinematics, use \( \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \) to find the speed at any position.

concepts.title: Internal Structure and Density
concepts.content_html:
Why does a steel ship float while a steel ball sinks? The answer lies in how mass is distributed — in other words, density.

Density

Density is mass per unit volume:

\[ \rho = \frac{m}{V} \]

SI units: kg/m³. Water's density is \( 1000 \) kg/m³ (or \( 1.0 \) g/cm³).

Density and Floating

  • Object sinks if \( \rho_{\text{object}} > \rho_{\text{fluid}} \)
  • Object floats if \( \rho_{\text{object}} < \rho_{\text{fluid}} \)
  • Object is neutrally buoyant if \( \rho_{\text{object}} = \rho_{\text{fluid}} \)

Internal Structure of Fluids

Fluids (liquids and gases) differ from solids in that their molecules can flow past one another. In a fluid at rest:

  • Molecules are in constant random motion
  • Intermolecular forces are weaker than in solids
  • Fluids conform to the shape of their container
  • Liquids are nearly incompressible; gases are highly compressible

Variable Definitions

  • \( \rho \) = density (kg/m³)
  • \( m \) = mass (kg)
  • \( V \) = volume (m³)

Worked Example

A block of wood has mass \( 0.60 \) kg and dimensions \( 0.10 \) m × \( 0.10 \) m × \( 0.10 \) m. What is its density? Will it float in water?

\[ V = 0.10 \times 0.10 \times 0.10 = 0.001 \text{ m³} \]

\[ \rho = \frac{0.60}{0.001} = 600 \text{ kg/m³} \]

Since \( 600 < 1000 \) kg/m³, the block floats in water.

Key Idea: Density determines whether an object floats or sinks. It's not about mass alone — a massive ship can float because its average density (including air space) is less than water.
AP Exam Tip: Be careful with units. Convert cm³ to m³ if needed (1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³). Also, remember that density is an intensive property — it doesn't depend on the amount of material.

concepts.title: Pressure
concepts.content_html:
Diving deeper into a pool, you feel increasing pressure on your ears. Pressure is one of the most important concepts in fluid mechanics.

Definition of Pressure

Pressure is force per unit area:

\[ P = \frac{F}{A} \]

SI unit: Pascal (Pa) = N/m². Atmospheric pressure at sea level: \( P_0 \approx 1.01 \times 10^5 \) Pa.

Pressure in a Fluid at Rest

Pressure increases with depth in a fluid due to the weight of the fluid above:

\[ P = P_0 + \rho g h \]

where \( P_0 \) is the pressure at the surface, \( \rho \) is the fluid density, \( g \) is gravitational acceleration, and \( h \) is the depth below the surface.

Key Properties of Fluid Pressure

  • Pressure acts in all directions equally at a given depth (Pascal's principle)
  • Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container
  • At the same depth in the same fluid, the pressure is the same everywhere

Gauge Pressure vs. Absolute Pressure

  • Absolute pressure: \( P = P_0 + \rho g h \)
  • Gauge pressure: \( P_{\text{gauge}} = \rho g h \) (pressure above atmospheric)

Variable Definitions

  • \( P \) = pressure (Pa = N/m²)
  • \( F \) = force (N)
  • \( A \) = area (m²)
  • \( P_0 \) = atmospheric pressure (\( \approx 1.01 \times 10^5 \) Pa)
  • \( h \) = depth (m)

Worked Example

What is the absolute pressure at \( 5.0 \) m below the surface of a lake?

\[ P = P_0 + \rho g h = 1.01 \times 10^5 + (1000)(9.8)(5.0) = 1.01 \times 10^5 + 4.9 \times 10^4 = 1.50 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa} \]

Key Idea: Pressure in a static fluid increases linearly with depth. At a given depth, pressure is the same in all directions and doesn't depend on container shape.
AP Exam Tip: Watch for whether a problem asks for gauge pressure (\( \rho gh \)) or absolute pressure (\( P_0 + \rho gh \)). Read carefully — the answers can differ by \( 10^5 \) Pa!

concepts.title: Fluids and Newton's Laws
concepts.content_html:
Why does a beach ball pop up from underwater? Why does a helium balloon rise? These are consequences of buoyancy, which arises directly from pressure differences in fluids.

Buoyant Force

Archimedes' Principle: The buoyant force on an object submerged (fully or partially) in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid displaced:

\[ F_b = \rho_f V_d g \]

where \( \rho_f \) is the fluid density, \( V_d \) is the volume of fluid displaced, and \( g \) is gravitational acceleration.

Origin of Buoyancy

Buoyancy arises because pressure increases with depth. The bottom of a submerged object experiences greater pressure (and thus greater upward force) than the top. The net upward force is the buoyant force.

Floating Objects

When an object floats, the buoyant force equals its weight:

\[ F_b = mg \implies \rho_f V_d g = \rho_{\text{obj}} V_{\text{obj}} g \]

\[ \frac{V_d}{V_{\text{obj}}} = \frac{\rho_{\text{obj}}}{\rho_f} \]

This tells us what fraction of the object is submerged.

Apparent Weight

An object submerged in a fluid appears to weigh less. The apparent weight is:

\[ W_{\text{app}} = mg - F_b \]

Variable Definitions

  • \( F_b \) = buoyant force (N)
  • \( \rho_f \) = fluid density (kg/m³)
  • \( V_d \) = displaced volume (m³)
  • \( W_{\text{app}} \) = apparent weight (N)

Worked Example

A block of wood (density \( 600 \) kg/m³) floats in water. What fraction is submerged?

\[ \frac{V_d}{V_{\text{obj}}} = \frac{\rho_{\text{obj}}}{\rho_f} = \frac{600}{1000} = 0.60 \]

60% of the block is submerged.

Key Idea: Buoyancy is caused by the pressure difference between the top and bottom of an object in a fluid. Archimedes' principle: \( F_b = \rho_f V_d g \) = weight of displaced fluid.
AP Exam Tip: For floating objects, \( F_b = mg \). The fraction submerged equals the ratio of densities. Don't forget: a fully submerged object displaces a volume equal to its own volume.

problems.question_html: Explain why buoyant force arises from pressure differences, not from a special 'buoyancy force.' Use a simple submerged cube as an example and show how the net upward force from pressure equals \( \rho_f V g \).
problems.sample_answer: Consider a cube of side length s submerged in a fluid with its top face at depth h and bottom face at depth h + s. Pressure on the top face: P_top = P₀ + ρfgh, pushing down with force F_top = P_top × s². Pressure on the bottom: P_bottom = P₀ + ρfg(h+s), pushing up with force F_bottom = P_bottom × s². The horizontal forces cancel by symmetry. Net upward force = F_bottom − F_top = ρfg(h+s)s² − ρfghs² = ρfgs³ = ρfgV. This is exactly Archimedes' principle. Buoyancy is not a separate force — it's the net result of fluid pressure acting on all surfaces of the submerged object.
rubric: Correctly identifies pressure at top and bottom faces of a submerged cube
Shows the net force calculation: F_bottom − F_top = ρfg(s³) = ρfgV
Explains that buoyancy is the net effect of pressure differences, not a separate force

Bottom face at depth \( h + s \): upward force = \( (P_0 + \rho g(h+s)) s^2 \).
Net upward = \( \rho g s \cdot s^2 = \rho g s^3 = \rho g V \). This is Archimedes' principle — buoyancy from pressure.

concepts.title: Fluids and Conservation Laws
concepts.content_html:
Water speeds up when a hose nozzle narrows. An airplane wing generates lift because air moves faster over the top. These phenomena involve the conservation of mass and energy applied to flowing fluids.

Equation of Continuity

For an incompressible fluid flowing through a pipe, the volume flow rate is constant:

\[ A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \]

where \( A \) is the cross-sectional area and \( v \) is the fluid speed. When the pipe narrows (\( A \) decreases), the fluid speeds up (\( v \) increases).

Bernoulli's Equation

Bernoulli's equation applies conservation of energy to a flowing fluid (ideal, incompressible, streamline flow):

\[ P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g y_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g y_2 \]

This says that along a streamline, the sum of pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume, and gravitational potential energy per unit volume is constant.

Key Implications

  • Where fluid speed is higher, pressure is lower (at the same height)
  • This explains lift on airplane wings, atomizers, and the curve of spinning balls

Variable Definitions

  • \( A \) = cross-sectional area (m²)
  • \( v \) = fluid speed (m/s)
  • \( P \) = pressure (Pa)
  • \( y \) = height (m)
  • \( \rho \) = fluid density (kg/m³)

Worked Example

Water flows through a pipe at \( 2.0 \) m/s in a section with area \( 0.040 \) m². The pipe narrows to \( 0.010 \) m². What is the speed in the narrow section?

\[ A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \implies v_2 = \frac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} = \frac{(0.040)(2.0)}{0.010} = 8.0 \text{ m/s} \]

Key Idea: The equation of continuity (conservation of mass) tells us fluid speeds up in narrow sections. Bernoulli's equation (conservation of energy) tells us pressure drops where speed increases.
AP Exam Tip: Bernoulli's equation applies to ideal (inviscid, incompressible, streamline) flow. Real fluids have viscosity and turbulence, but for AP Physics 1, the ideal model is sufficient.

problems.question_html: Use the equation of continuity and Bernoulli's principle to explain why a garden hose sprays water faster when you partially cover the opening with your thumb. Include both the effect on speed and on pressure.
problems.sample_answer: By covering part of the opening, you reduce the exit area A₂. The equation of continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) tells us that if A₂ decreases while the flow rate stays approximately constant, v₂ must increase. The water exits at a higher speed, allowing it to spray farther. From Bernoulli's equation (P + ½ρv² = constant at the same height), the increased speed at the exit means the pressure there is lower. The higher pressure inside the hose (behind your thumb) pushes the water out at the increased speed. Essentially, covering the opening converts pressure energy into kinetic energy of the water.

Continuity: \( A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \). Smaller \( A_2 \) → larger \( v_2 \).
Bernoulli: higher speed → lower pressure at exit. The pressure difference between inside and outside the hose accelerates the water to a higher exit speed.
